vignette:
Rana is a 51-year-old hotel manager at a large downtown property. She has held this position for nearly twelve years, overseeing a staff of over eighty housekeepers, front desk agents, and maintenance workers. She is married to Tariq, a civil engineer, and they have two grown children living abroad. Rana describes herself as someone who "used to be calm under pressure" and proud of her ability to handle crisis situations. That changed two years ago, on a Tuesday in late August.

The hotel's pool maintenance crew had been using a concentrated chlorine-based algaecide in an enclosed pump room. A faulty valve released a plume of toxic gas into the adjacent storage corridor where Rana was inspecting linens. She remembers the smell first-sharp, biting, like bleach mixed with burning metal. Her eyes immediately stung, and her chest tightened. She stumbled out, gasping, coughing so hard she vomited. Three housekeepers were also affected. The fire department arrived, the building was evacuated, and she was treated at the emergency room for acute chemical inhalation. Physically, she recovered within a week. But the chemical smell never really left her.

Now, in the present, Rana avoids the lower-level corridor entirely. She takes the long way around, adding fifteen minutes to her morning walkthrough. She has delegated all pool area inspections to her assistant. If a guest complains about a chlorine smell near the spa, she feels her throat close up and her heart race. She has instructed housekeeping to use only unscented cleaning products, and she personally checks every new shipment for any bleach or ammonia-based contents. Her staff has noticed. They whisper that she "has become too controlling." Rana knows this. She cannot explain why the smell of a lemon-scented floor cleaner makes her dizzy and sends her to the bathroom to splash water on her face.

At home, things are quieter but not easier. She flinches when Tariq uses bleach to clean the bathroom. She has asked him to stop, but he does not always remember. She has stopped cooking certain foods because the sizzle of onions in oil reminds her of the hiss of the valve. She sleeps poorly, waking at 3 a.m. with her lungs tight and her mind replaying the moment she could not find the door handle. She has started drinking two glasses of wine most nights to help herself fall asleep. Tariq has asked if she wants to talk about it. She says she is fine. He has stopped asking.

At work, Rana is efficient but brittle. She snaps at employees who leave cleaning carts near the mechanical rooms. She feels a constant, low-level dread that another leak could happen at any moment. She checks the chemical storage logs twice a day. She cannot walk past a janitor's closet without holding her breath. During a recent fire drill, she became so dizzy and short of breath that the safety officer had to help her sit down. She told him it was low blood sugar.

She avoids reading the news about chemical spills or industrial accidents. She has changed the route she drives home to avoid a road near a water treatment plant. She has not visited the hotel pool in over a year. When a guest left a positive review online mentioning the "fresh, clean smell of the lobby," Rana had to leave her desk and walk outside.

She tells me, in session, that she wishes she could just "get over it." She does not connect the dots between the panic and the exposure. She believes she is weak, that other people would have handled it better. She holds herself to the standard of the hotel manager she used to be. That version of Rana is still there, she insists-just buried under the weight of a smell she cannot escape.
